record.title: Deep Noir reports automated activation steering and task-dependent injection risks
record.summary: The Deep Noir preprint combines Logit Lens timing with causal head attribution to search for activation-steering parameters. The authors report gains on spam and sentiment classification across selected 1B–9B research models, including +16.7 percentage points on spam at 1B and +13.1 points on SST-2 sentiment in the stated setup. They also report that steering magnitude and injection success move together in some model/task settings. The paper's own results are architecture- and task-dependent: steering reduces injection vulnerability in one 7B result and reverses direction for two of three models on a sentiment-adapted attack. These are author-reported findings, not an independent reproduction or evidence of an attack on deployed agents.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that Deep Noir combines Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to discover activation-steering parameters, improving SMS spam classification by 16.7 percentage points on a 1B model (±4.7, 39 runs), with reported gains of +21–42 points across four 7–9B architectures. They also report a +13.1-point SST-2 sentiment gain in the stated 1B setup.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper's prompt-injection evaluation, steering magnitude was associated with monotonically non-decreasing injection success for the evaluated OLMo and Gemma settings; the authors report OLMo rising from 0.34 at zero steering to 1.0 at 4×M*, and Gemma from 0.25 to 0.99.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The security effect was not uniform: the paper reports that steering reduced injection vulnerability from 97.5% to 61.1% for 7B Mistral, and that sentiment-adapted attacks moved in opposite directions for two of three models. The evidence therefore supports task- and architecture-dependent risk, not a universal increase in vulnerability.

contradictory_evidence: The paper's security findings are not monotonic across tasks and architectures: two of three sentiment-adapted models move in opposite directions, and the 7B Mistral result shows lower injection vulnerability after steering. This constrains the abstract's broader attack-surface framing to specific evaluated settings.

evidence_gaps.description: The activation-steering, cross-task and prompt-injection results have not been independently reproduced, and no author-linked code artifact was located in the inspected paper.
Transfer from small research-model classifiers to systems that route requests or authorize agent actions is not measured.

brief.importance_rationale: If the paper's bounded results reproduce, mechanistic activation steering could automate task-specific classifier interventions while changing prompt-injection susceptibility in some evaluated settings. The results cover research models through 9B, selected classification tasks and author-run trials; the importance is notable for steering evaluation and security, not evidence of deployed-agent compromise.
limitations: All reported results are from one preprint and were not independently reproduced; no code artifact was located in the inspected source.

The evaluations use selected research-model classifiers through 9B and a small set of spam, sentiment and injection benchmarks; they do not demonstrate safety or compromise outcomes in deployed agents.

The paper reports architecture- and task-dependent effects: cross-task attack results reverse for two of three models, and steering reduces injection vulnerability in the 7B Mistral result. The monotonic-with-magnitude result is limited to the evaluated OLMo/Gemma settings.
The authors use custom steering, coherence and attack metrics; their independent validity and transfer to other models, prompts and deployment controls remain unknown.
Near-chance 1B MMLU baselines make some reported containment deltas noisy; statistical and practical significance should not be inferred beyond the paper's stated comparisons.
brief.summary: The Deep Noir preprint combines Logit Lens timing with causal head attribution to search for activation-steering parameters. The authors report gains on spam and sentiment classification across selected 1B–9B research models, including +16.7 percentage points on spam at 1B and +13.1 points on SST-2 sentiment in the stated setup. They also report that steering magnitude and injection success move together in some model/task settings. The paper's own results are architecture- and task-dependent: steering reduces injection vulnerability in one 7B result and reverses direction for two of three models on a sentiment-adapted attack. These are author-reported findings, not an independent reproduction or evidence of an attack on deployed agents.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report automated parameter discovery and classification gains across selected Llama, OLMo, Gemma and Mistral models. Their injection results vary with architecture, task, model scale and steering magnitude; they argue that the curve can inform configuration selection, but the study does not test deployed agents or tool authorization systems.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports discovery times of 4–10 minutes at 1B, about 15 minutes at 3B and about 30 minutes at 7B. Hardware and complete end-to-end costs were not independently checked in this review.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint reports +16.7 percentage points on spam at 1B (±4.7 across 39 runs), +21–42 points on spam across four 7–9B architectures, and +13.1 points on SST-2 sentiment in the stated setup. It also reports OLMo/Gemma injection increases with steering magnitude in tested settings, alongside a reduction from 97.5% to 61.1% for 7B Mistral. All results are author-reported; the research desk did not reproduce them.
technical.implementation_status: Preprint experiments only; no deployed agent integration or independently executed implementation was verified.
technical.mechanism: The paper uses Logit Lens convergence to locate where concepts resolve through model layers, then causal head-level attribution to rank intervention points and search steering magnitude. It applies selected activation directions to spam and sentiment classifiers and evaluates both task accuracy and prompt-injection behavior.
technical.novelty: Composes layer-wise timing diagnostics with causal head attribution to automate a steering search, and evaluates classification performance and injection susceptibility under the resulting interventions.
technical.regime: Author-run classification experiments on selected 1B, 2–3B and 7–9B research-model families; SMS spam and SST-2 sentiment; injection tests using 24 templates over 50 emails (3,600 trials), sentiment-adapted tests and selected public benchmarks. Results are task- and architecture-specific.
technical.reproducibility: The current arXiv record is v1. No author-linked implementation artifact was located in the inspected paper, and the research desk did not reproduce the experiments or independently audit the custom metrics.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares Deep Noir with baseline classifiers, random search and RepE steering without head masking. The authors report RepE matching baseline on SST-2 in the stated folds while Deep Noir improves; the research desk did not verify the statistical analysis or rerun the comparisons.

brief.title: Deep Noir reports automated activation steering and task-dependent injection risks
brief.why_it_matters: Mechanistic activation steering may automate interventions that otherwise require manual layer and magnitude selection. The same intervention can alter how a classifier responds to prompt injections, so accuracy gains and attack behavior need to be measured together. The preprint reports both effects, but its small-model classification regimes and mixed cross-task results do not establish generalization to deployed agent systems.
